There are various types of Pronouns:

Personal pronouns: stand in for a person—"Bill did it. He was there."
Demonstrative pronouns: point to a person or object which is near (this/these) or far (that/those).
Relative pronouns: relate a subordinate clause to a noun—"It is a great person who attempts to master Greek."
Reciprocal pronouns: state an interchange between two things/persons—They loved one another.
Reflexive pronouns: direct the action of the verb back to the subject—"She hid herself behind the door."
Interrogative pronouns: ask a question—Who broke the chair?

320.heading: Introduction
320.text:
Introduction

Personal pronouns in Greek will match their antecedent in person, gender, and number. The case will be determined by the role the pronoun plays in the sentence.

Personal pronouns will be either first person (I, we), second person (you), or third person (he/she/it/they).

Greek will use the genitive where we would normally use a possessive pronoun (e.g. his, her).

Since the nominative is indicated in the personal ending of the verb (e.g. λέγω = I say) when the personal pronoun is used it is for emphasis (e.g. ἐγὼ λέγω = I say).

In the first and second person there are emphatic forms. These are usually the forms used in prepositional phrases.

topics.heading: Enclitics
topics.text:
Enclitics

An enclitic is a word that is phonetically attached so closely with the word that precedes it that it has no accent of its own. Many personal pronouns are enclitics (e.g. μου, μοι, με, σου, σοι, σε).

Enclitics are sometimes accented:

for emphasis
when the first word in a sentence.

If the preceding word has an acute on the antepenult or a circumflex on the penult, a second accent will be added on the ultima. This results in the word preceding the enclitic being double accented.

ἄνθρωπός μου
my man
δῶρόν σου
your gift

Finally, an acute on the ultima is not changed to a grave before an enclitic.

topics.heading: Enclitics
topics.text:
Enclitics

An enclitic is a word that is phonetically attached so closely with the word that precedes it that it has no accent of its own. Many personal pronouns are enclitics (e.g. μου, μοι, με, σου, σοι, σε).

Enclitics are sometimes accented:

for emphasis
when the first word in a sentence.

If the preceding word has an acute on the antepenult or a circumflex on the penult, a second accent will be added on the ultima. This results in the word preceding the enclitic being double accented.

ἄνθρωπός μου
my man
δῶρόν σου
your gift

Finally, an acute on the ultima is not changed to a grave before an enclitic.
